caption:
Mortgage renewal London Ontario 2027: three neighbours renew, and only one payment jumps.
Dan Balch, Licensed Mortgage Broker · Lic. M08003485 · Mortgage Architects · Brokerage Lic. #12728

Illustrative example. Three London neighbours each borrowed $500,000 over 25 years.
A signed a 5-year fixed in Feb 2022 at 2.81%.
B signed a 5-year fixed in Nov 2022 at 5.17%.
C signed a 3-year fixed in Mar 2024 at 5.43%.
(Those are Bank of Canada monthly averages for new uninsured fixed mortgages.)

All three renew in 2027. At 4.66%, the September 2026 average for a new 5-year fixed, and with the same years left:
A: $2,318 to $2,720 a month (+$402)
B: $2,957 to $2,835 (−$122)
C: $3,032 to $2,832 (−$200)

The rule behind it: keep the same years left, and your payment goes up only if you renew above the rate you signed. Rates have moved since September, so check your own number.

A smaller payment still isn't a reason to sign the first offer. On B's balance, each 0.25% is about $59 a month. Moving to another lender at renewal with the same balance and amortization doesn't need a new stress test, though the new lender still has to approve you.

Renewing in London or Komoka in 2027? Send this to the neighbour who signed in early 2022.

Illustrative market averages, not an offer or advice. Semi-annual compounding, payments rounded to the dollar. Your rate, term and APR depend on your lender and approval. Sources: Bank of Canada mortgage rate data (to Sep 2026, retrieved Nov 19, 2026); OSFI straight-switch exemption (Nov 21, 2024).

math.claim: Composite inputs: each neighbour borrowed $500,000 over 25 years (slide 1 {principal}/{amort}, all assumptions lines)
math.working: Illustrative composite, not a real client. Slide 1 calc payment {principal:500000, annualPct:2.81, amortYears:25} prints $500,000 and 25.
Bank of Canada Valet V122667786 and V122667785, effective rate on new uninsured fixed mortgages, re-pulled 2026-11-19; latest observation 2026-09-01 = 4.66%

math.claim: Balances at renewal: A $425,802 (20 yrs left), B $443,711 (20 yrs left), C $469,048 (22 yrs left)
math.working: Semi-annual compounding: i = (1 + r/200)^(1/6) − 1; pmt = P·i/(1−(1+i)^−300); balance after k payments = P(1+i)^k − pmt((1+i)^k − 1)/i. A: k=60 at 2.81% = 425,801.72. B: k=60 at 5.17% = 443,710.91. C: k=36 at 5.43% = 469,048.47 (Python-checked).

math.claim: A: $2,318 now, $2,720 at renewal, $402 more a month
math.working: Payment on 425,801.72 over 20 yrs at 2.81% = 2,317.75 (equals the original payment on $500,000/25 yrs, as it must); at 4.66% = 2,720.43. Rounded 2,720 − 2,318 = 402 (exact 402.67, +17.4%). calc.mjs fills: a $2,318, b $2,720, delta $402.

math.claim: B: $2,957 now, $2,835 at renewal, $122 less a month
math.working: Payment on 443,710.91 over 20 yrs at 5.17% = 2,956.60 (= original); at 4.66% = 2,834.85. Rounded 2,957 − 2,835 = 122 (exact 121.75). Reversed second calc gives {delta} $122.

math.claim: C: $3,032 now, $2,832 at renewal, $200 less a month
Slide 6 rule: with the same years left, the payment rises only if the renewal rate is above the signed rate
math.working: The remaining balance re-amortized over the remaining years at the original rate reproduces the original payment exactly (checked: 2,317.75 / 2,956.60 / 3,031.61). Payment rises with rate, so break-even is the signed rate: A 2.81%, B 5.17%, C 5.43%.

math.claim: Slide 7: each 0.25% on B's balance is about $59 a month
Slide 8: start shopping about 120 days out
